elements.id-string-15: Structured product data in the form of attribute/value pairs is the foundation of many e-commerce applications such as faceted product search, product comparison, and product recommendation.
elements.id-string-16: Product offers often only contain textual descriptions of the product attributes in the form of titles or free text.
elements.id-string-17: Hence, extracting attribute/value pairs from textual product descriptions is an essential enabler for e-commerce applications.In order to excel, state-of-the-art product information extraction methods require large quantities of task-specific training data.
elements.id-string-18: The methods also struggle with generalizing to out-of-distribution attributes and attribute values that were not a part of the training data.Due to being pre-trained on huge amounts of text as well as due to emergent effects resulting from the model size, Large Language Models like ChatGPT have the potential to address both of these shortcomings.This paper explores the potential of ChatGPT for extracting attribute/value pairs from product descriptions.
elements.id-string-19: We experiment with different zero-shot and few-shot prompt designs.Our results show that ChatGPT achieves a performance similar to a pre-trained language model but requires much smaller amounts of training data and computation for fine-tuning.
elements.id-string-20: \keywords{Product Information Extraction, Large Language Models, ChatGPT}
elements.id-string-22: Product attribute/value pairs are crucial for e-commerce platforms since they enable online shoppers to use faceted product search~\cite{wei_survey_2013} and to compare products along explicit criteria.
elements.id-string-23: On e-commerce marketplaces and open product catalogues, product attribute/value pairs are often missing because merchants only provide unstructured product information, such as titles and descriptions~\cite{yang_mave_2022,zheng_opentag_2018}.
elements.id-string-24: Product information extraction extracts attribute/value pairs from these product titles and product descriptions.
elements.id-string-25: Existing works can be distinguished into closed extraction and open extraction approaches.
elements.id-string-26: Closed extraction assumes that the relevant attributes are known prior to the extraction ~\cite{yang_mave_2022, zheng_opentag_2018, zhu_multimodal_2020, xu_scaling_2019, wang_learning_2020}.
elements.id-string-27: Open extraction assumes that neither a complete attribute set nor all attribute values are known prior to the extraction~\cite{zhang_oa-mine_2022}.
elements.id-string-28: For example, consider the following title of a product offer \emph{``Canon EOS 1000D SLR 10 MP EF-S 18-55''}.
elements.id-string-29: A closed extraction approach extracts from this title an explicit attribute like \emph{``Resolution``} and returns the attribute/value pair \emph{``Resolution: 10 MP``}.
elements.id-string-30: An open extraction extracts all attribute/value pairs and returns a list of attribute/value pairs like \emph{``Brand: Canon``, ``Megapixels: 10``}.
elements.id-string-32: Many state-of-the-art product information extraction methods~\cite{zhu_multimodal_2020, xu_scaling_2019, yang_mave_2022, zheng_opentag_2018}rely on pre-trained language models (PLM) such as BERT.The different approaches encode a product title using the PLM and add additional layers on top, which tag the sequence of an attribute value in the title.OA-Mine is an example of an open extraction approach that relies on a PLM to generate attribute value candidates from product titles and to discover new attributes from the generated attribute value candidates~\cite{zhang_oa-mine_2022}.The approaches have two main drawbacks: (1) they require training data to fine-tune the models, and (2) the fine-tuned models have problems generalizing to unseen attributes and attribute values.
elements.id-string-33: Large autoregressive language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT~\cite{ouyang_training_2022}, BLOOM~\cite{yong_bloom1_2023} or PaLM~\cite{chowdhery_palm_2022} have recently shown their potential to overcome these shortcomings.
elements.id-string-34: Due to being pre-trained on huge amounts of text as well as due to emergent effects resulting from the model size~\cite{wei_emergent_2022}, LLMs often demonstrate a better zero-shot performance compared to PLMs like BERT and are more robust to unseen examples~\cite{brown_language_2020}.
elements.id-string-35: In this paper, we evaluate how ChatGPT extracts attribute/value pairs from product titles using prompt engineering and in-context learning
elements.id-string-38: We evaluate the performance of ChatGPT (gpt3.5-turbo-0301) for closed and open product information extraction.We systematically explore different prompt designs and show the performance of the best zero-shot prompt design is similar to a fine-tuned pre-trained language model.We experiment with in-context learning for product information extraction and show that providing only three demonstrations is sufficient to reach an F1 score of 94.51\%.

elements.id-string-44: In this section, we introduce our experimental setup.
elements.id-string-45: For this setup, we discuss the MAVE dataset and how we prepared it for our experiments, the API calls against the OpenAI API, the evaluation and the baselines.
elements.id-string-47: We experimented with a subset of product titles from the MAVE dataset~\cite{yang_mave_2022}.
elements.id-string-48: MAVE is a product dataset for multi-source attribute value extraction.
elements.id-string-49: MAVE is derived from a public collection of product offers from the e-commerce platform Amazon~\cite{ni_justifying_2019}.
elements.id-string-50: The authors of MAVE add annotations of attribute/value pairs for attribute values that can be found in the product titles and descriptions.
elements.id-string-51: To obtain these annotations, human experts define a set of categories and a list of attributes that are relevant for each category.
elements.id-string-52: Afterwards, each product offer is assigned to a product category and category-specific attribute value spans are annotated in the titles and descriptions of the product offers.
elements.id-string-53: An ensemble of five differently fine-tuned versions of the AVEQA~\cite{wang_learning_2020} model is used for this annotation.
elements.id-string-54: Each final record contains a single product offer with a product title, a product description, an attribute and annotation information about attribute values in the title or the description.
elements.id-string-55: Each record is attribute-dependent because a product offer can appear multiple times with different product attributes.
elements.id-string-56: The MAVE dataset contains in total 3.5 million unique products, 4.8 million unique attribute/value pairs, 2.4 thousand unique categories and 1.4 thousand unique attributes.
elements.id-string-58: In order to keep the costs of experimenting with the OpenAI API manageable, we restrict our experiments to a subset of product offers.
elements.id-string-59: The product offers are drawn from three selected product categories and have at least one annotation for one of 15 selected attributes.

elements.id-string-92: We train two closed extraction models as baselines for our experiments.
elements.id-string-93: Both baseline models rely on a PLM.
elements.id-string-94: The first baseline is a fully-trained AVEQA~\cite{wang_learning_2020} model, using 71,266 training records.
elements.id-string-95: AVEQA formulates the attribute/value pair extraction as a question-answering task.
elements.id-string-96: The model encodes both attribute and product title with a BERT encoder and predicts the attribute value.
elements.id-string-97: The model is fine-tuned for 20 epochs on the reduced MAVE training set with a learning rate of 3e-5 and a batch size of 32.
elements.id-string-98: The second baseline is a named entity recognition model (NER) for product attribute extraction~\cite{putthividhya_bootstrapped_2011}.
elements.id-string-99: For this NER model, we group the training set by product offer resulting in 18,083 records for training.
elements.id-string-100: DeBERTa is used to tokenize and encode the product titles~\cite {he_deberta_2021}.
elements.id-string-101: The tokens are annotated such that the model learns to classify tokens that describe an attribute value as mentioned in the training set.
elements.id-string-102: The model is fine-tuned for 10 epochs on the reduced MAVE training set with a learning rate of 2e-5 and a batch size of 8.
elements.id-string-103: Note that both baselines are fully trained over thousands of samples and their training took hours ($\sim$10 hrs.

elements.id-string-110: LLMs like ChatGPT expect text as input and return text as output.
elements.id-string-111: The input text is also known as a prompt.
elements.id-string-112: In our case, the prompt contains a task description and a task input.
elements.id-string-113: Recent work has shown that careful prompt design is crucial to achieving good performance~\cite{narayan_can_2022, zhao_calibrate_2021}.
elements.id-string-114: In this section, we experiment with different prompt designs to explore the zero-shot performance of ChatGPT.
elements.id-string-115: The prompt designs for product information extraction can be categorized into closed and open.
elements.id-string-116: We first introduce the closed and open prompt designs and afterwards present results.
elements.id-string-118: The goal of our closed prompts is to extract the value of a specific attribute from a product title.
elements.id-string-119: The task descriptions of closed product information prompts are categorized as follows:
elements.id-string-120: \textbf{Simple}: Task description asks for an attribute using simple language.\textbf{Request}: Task description requests a specific attribute.\textbf{Short answer (sh.)}: Task description asks the model to respond only with the attribute value.\textbf{Unknown (unk.)}: Task description tells the model how to answer if the attribute value cannot be derived.\textbf{Generated Knowledge}: Task description asks the model to first implicitly extract all attribute-value pairs before extracting an explicit attribute~\cite{liu_generated_2022}.
elements.id-string-121: We refer to a prompt that combines request, short and unknown as \textbf{Explicit}.
elements.id-string-122: The prompts (a), (b) and (c) in Figure \ref{fig:extraction_prompt_new} are example prompts for closed extraction: (a) is a simple prompt, (b) is an explicit prompt,
elements.id-string-123: and (c) is a prompt that uses generated knowledge.
elements.id-string-125: The goal of our open prompts is to extract all attribute-value pairs from a product title.
elements.id-string-126: Prompt (d) in Figure \ref{fig:extraction_prompt_new} shows an example prompt of open extraction.
elements.id-string-127: We explicitly describe the output format so that  attribute/value pairs can be parsed from the response and compared to the ground truth in the test set.
elements.id-string-129: Table \ref{tab:zero_shot_results} shows the results of all zero-shot prompts and baselines.
elements.id-string-130: Overall, our results show that ChatGPT achieves
elements.id-string-131: comparable performance to that of NER.
elements.id-string-132: AVEQA shows an exceptional performance with almost perfect Precision, Recall and F1
elements.id-string-133: and clearly outperforms the zero-shot results with ChatGPT.
elements.id-string-134: However, both baselines (AVEQA and NER) are finetuned on 71,266 attribute/value pairs and require additional computing for fine-tuning whereas ChatGPT needs only an explicit prompt.
elements.id-string-135: Requiring no training data for task-specific finetuning to achieve these results is an advantage of ChatGPT over AVEQA and NER.
elements.id-string-136: The explicit prompt (Explicit) with a request for an attribute, a short answer and telling the model how to respond (recall prompt example in Figure~\ref{fig:extraction_prompt_new}(b)) achieves an F1 score of 87.86\%.
elements.id-string-137: Specifically, telling the model how to respond if the attribute is unknown to the model, highly impacts the model's precision.
elements.id-string-138: Without 'unk.' the model's precision drops by 24.79\%.
elements.id-string-139: Generating knowledge about the product improves the results only marginally in our experiments and since the task descriptions are longer, costs more per Title.
elements.id-string-140: The open extraction is comparable to the best closed extraction results with respect to precision but the recall is more than 40\% lower.
elements.id-string-141: ChatGPT has no guidance on how the attributes are named and, thus, proposes its own attribute names.
elements.id-string-142: Since we check for an exact match on the attribute names during the evaluation, the unknown attribute names generated by ChatGPT are not found.
elements.id-string-143: Prompt (d) in Figure \ref{fig:extraction_prompt_new} illustrates this behaviour for the attribute \emph{"Resolution"}, which is extracted as \emph{"Megapixels"} by ChatGPT.
elements.id-string-144: A possible solution to this issue is to use demonstrations with an example schema, which ChatGPT can use to build a schema for the extraction.

elements.id-string-154: In-context learning is a paradigm that allows language models to learn a task based on a few example inputs and outputs also called demonstrations~\cite{brown_language_2020,dong_survey_2023}.
elements.id-string-155: In the context of this paper, we combine the closed prompt `Generated Knowledge` and the open prompt with demonstrations to analyze the impact of demonstrations on the performance of ChatGPT for Product Information Extraction.
elements.id-string-157: we explain how the demonstrations are selected and combined with the prompts.
elements.id-string-158: Then, we present the results of our experiments.
elements.id-string-160: The source for the used demonstrations is the reduced training set.
elements.id-string-161: Demonstrations are useful if they are semantically similar to the final task~\cite{liu_what_2022}.
elements.id-string-162: Since we know the product category of the input product title and assume that product offers with the same product category are semantically similar, the selected demonstrations are drawn from the same product category as the product offer for which we run the product information extraction.
elements.id-string-163: Both the closed and the open prompt are combined with one, three and six demonstrations.
elements.id-string-164: For the prompts with three and six demonstrations, two-thirds of the demonstrations are product offers where the value of the attribute/value pair is contained in the title and one-third are product offers where the value of the attribute/value pair is not contained in the title.
elements.id-string-165: This selection of demonstrations covers different possible structures of the task~\cite{levy_diverse_2022}.
elements.id-string-166: All attribute values of the demonstrations are manually checked and normalized like the examples listed in Table \ref{tab:value_normalization}.
elements.id-string-167: \vspace{.2cm}\textbf{Combination of Prompts and Demonstrations.} For the in-context learning prompts, we first provide the task description and add the task demonstrations.
elements.id-string-168: Each task demonstration consists of an example input and an example output.
elements.id-string-169: Afterwards, we repeat the task description and add the task input.

elements.id-string-174: The results with in-context learning in Table \ref{tab:few_shot_results} show that demonstrations improve the extraction of attribute/value pairs of closed and open prompts.
elements.id-string-175: A single example (one-shot) is already sufficient to increase the closed extraction results by 4.24\% in terms of F1.
elements.id-string-176: Additional demonstrations add another 1-2\% in F1, with a maximal F1 of 94.51 achieved with (only) six samples.
elements.id-string-177: The open extraction benefits the most from the demonstrations.
elements.id-string-178: A single example is sufficient to increase the performance of ChatGPT by almost 33\% in terms of F1.
elements.id-string-179: We noticed that the model picks up on the structure of the demonstrations and uses the demonstration attribute/value pairs to extract the attribute/value pairs from the task input.
elements.id-string-180: Looking at the example prompt (f) in Figure \ref{fig:few_shot_cropped}, for example, the model learns from the task demonstration that the attribute value \emph{"10 MP"} has to be extracted as \emph{"Resolution: 10 MP"}, rather than \emph{"Megapixels: 10 MP"} as it can happen if no demonstration is provided.
elements.id-string-181: In our experiments, open extraction prompts with three and six demonstrations resulted in a worse performance than experiments with only one demonstration.
elements.id-string-182: We assume that this behaviour is caused by the longer prompts but additional experiments are necessary to verify this hypothesis.
elements.id-string-184: On the one hand, the closed extraction few-shot prompts are 25\% cheaper per API call and exhibit an 8\% higher F1 recall than the open extraction few-shot prompts.
elements.id-string-185: On the other hand, open extraction prompts can extract multiple attributes, which makes them cheaper than closed extraction prompts if two or more attributes have to be extracted.
elements.id-string-187: In this paper, we systematically evaluate ChatGPT(gpt3.5-turbo-0301) for the task of product information extraction.
elements.id-string-188: We experiment with different zero-shot prompt designs, which show that a proper prompt design is sufficient to achieve similar performance to that of a fine-tuned NER baseline.
elements.id-string-189: By adding demonstrations to the prompts, the results are further improved.
